title: 2 Kings 25:1–12
context: In Zedekiah’s ninth year Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem; by the eleventh year famine grips the city, the wall is breached, and the king flees but is captured near Jericho. At Riblah his sons are killed before him, he is blinded and taken to Babylon, and a month later Nebuzaradan burns the temple, the palace, and the houses, breaks down the walls, and deports the people, leaving some of the poorest to work the land. Both traditions read these events soberly as shared ground.

verses.text: In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem, and encamped against it; and they built forts against it around it.
verses.arminianNotes:
“In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note the precise dating, which Jeremiah 39:1 and 52:4 also record.

The careful date marks the gravity of the event.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the date recorded as a turning point in Judah’s history.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the siege begins the final stage of the judgment that the LORD had announced through his prophets.

verses.text: So the city was besieged until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So the city was besieged until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.” Arminian readers note the length of the siege.

The narrator reports the duration plainly, without describing its suffering in detail.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a prolonged siege in which the city had time to heed the prophets’ counsel (cf. Jer 38:17).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the delay of the final blow is part of the narrative’s sober account.

verses.text: On the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine was severe in the city, so that there was no bread for the people of the land.
verses.arminianNotes:
“On the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine was severe in the city, so that there was no bread for the people of the land.” Arminian readers note the suffering of ordinary people in the siege.

Jeremiah 39:2 and 52:6 give the same date.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the famine as part of the covenant curses warned of long before (cf. Lev 26:26).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground and read it with compassion: the people of the land bore the hardship of the city’s fall.

verses.text: Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled by night by the way of the gate between the two walls, which was by the king’s garden (now the Chaldeans were against the city around it); and the king went by the way of the Arabah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled by night by the way of the gate between the two walls.” Arminian readers note the collapse of the defense and the flight of the soldiers.

The king goes “by the way of the Arabah.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the city’s defenses fail at last.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the king and his warriors could not escape what the LORD had spoken (cf. Jer 38:18).

verses.text: But the Chaldean army pursued the king, and overtook him in the plains of Jericho; and all his army was scattered from him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But the Chaldean army pursued the king, and overtook him in the plains of Jericho; and all his army was scattered from him.” Arminian readers note that his flight fails.

The scattering recalls Micaiah’s image of sheep without a shepherd (1 Kings 22:17).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the king abandoned by his army as his attempt to escape collapses.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: human plans cannot overturn the judgment announced through the prophets.

verses.text: Then they captured the king and carried him up to the king of Babylon to Riblah; and they passed judgment on him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then they captured the king and carried him up to the king of Babylon to Riblah; and they passed judgment on him.” Arminian readers note that Zedekiah had broken his oath of loyalty (cf. 2 Chr 36:13).

The judgment at Riblah is reported briefly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Zedekiah facing the consequences of his rebellion.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the king is held responsible, and the narrator records the judgment without elaboration.

verses.text: They killed Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, then put out Zedekiah’s eyes, bound him in fetters, and carried him to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They killed Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, then put out Zedekiah’s eyes, bound him in fetters, and carried him to Babylon.” Arminian readers read this soberly as a grievous end to Judah’s last king.

The text reports the events briefly, and readers should not add detail.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers read it with the same sobriety. Some readers connect the verse with Ezekiel 12:13 and Jeremiah 34:3, which spoke of Zedekiah being taken to Babylon.

Both traditions grieve the loss and treat the verse as shared ground on the cost of rebellion against God’s word.

verses.text: Now in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, which was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, which was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar.” Arminian readers note the careful date of Nebuzaradan’s arrival.

Jeremiah 52:12 gives the tenth day of the month; the difference is noted without resolution.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the precise date and the difference with Jeremiah 52:12.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the arrival of the captain of the guard marks the final destruction of the city.

verses.text: He burned the LORD’s house, the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem. He burned every great house with fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He burned the LORD’s house, the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note the end of the temple Solomon built.

The narrator reports the burning plainly; books such as Lamentations express the grief that followed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the fulfillment of the warning that the LORD would cast off the house where his name dwelt (23:27).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the loss of the temple was real and grievous, yet God’s presence was not confined to a building (cf. 1 Kings 8:27).

verses.text: All the army of the Chaldeans, who were with the captain of the guard, broke down the walls around Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All the army of the Chaldeans, who were with the captain of the guard, broke down the walls around Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note the city’s complete loss of defense.

The broken walls later become a concern in Nehemiah’s day (Neh 1:3).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the demolition as completing the judgment on the city.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, read soberly: Jerusalem is left without walls or protection.

verses.text: Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive the rest of the people who were left in the city and those who had deserted to the king of Babylon—all the rest of the multitude.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nebuzaradan carries away “the rest of the people who were left in the city and those who had deserted to the king of Babylon—all the rest of the multitude.” Arminian readers note that even those who surrendered go into exile.

Jeremiah 52:28–30 gives figures for the deportations.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the scope of the exile reaching nearly all who remained in the city.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the deportation fulfills the warnings of exile (cf. Deut 28:36).

verses.text: But the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to work the vineyards and fields.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to work the vineyards and fields.” Arminian readers note that the land is not left entirely empty.

Jeremiah 39:10 adds that he gave them vineyards and fields.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a remnant left in the land even in judgment.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the poorest receive land to work, a small note of provision within the disaster.
